section_summary: This section traces the consolidation of Japan’s English-language press, especially the Japanese government’s alleged support of the Japan Times and the pressured sales of the American-owned Japan Advertiser and British-owned Japan Chronicle. It then examines the independent Japan News-Week, its American ownership, financial and censorship difficulties, anti-Axis stance, and importance as a vehicle for American viewpoints. The final pages reproduce or summarize editorials criticizing the Tripartite Alliance, Japanese expansionism, Axis strategy, and aspects of United States policy while urging a peaceful Japanese-American settlement.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 4585: Information with Regard to the English Language Press in Tokyo
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports alleged Japanese Foreign Ministry control of the Japan Times and efforts by Japanese, German, and British interests to acquire the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports information that the Japanese Foreign Ministry controls and subsidizes the Japan Times, where Toshi Go recently replaced Hitoshi Ashida and began recruiting American journalists. Go’s official career and the newspaper’s pro-Japanese presentation of the “New Order in East Asia” are offered as evidence of the paper’s semi-official character. The despatch also reviews unsuccessful Japanese, German, and British approaches to the American owners of the Japan Advertiser.

subfiles.title: Ashida Resigns as President, Editor of Times
subfiles.about: Announces Hitoshi Ashida’s resignation and Toshi Go’s appointment as managing director and editor of the Japan Times.
subfiles.summary: The article states that Ashida is leaving journalism to devote more attention to his Seiyukai Party duties. It presents Go’s service in government, international conferences, the South Manchuria Railway, and the New York World’s Fair as qualifications for directing the paper and addressing Japanese-American relations.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Negotiations for Disposal of the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: Relays Wilfrid Fleisher’s confidential account of competing proposals and Japanese pressure concerning the sale of the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: Benjamin Fleisher wants to sell the paper and return to the U.S. but rejects German and British embassy arrangements; a Japanese group under Toshi Go offered about half his $400,000 price, reportedly warning the government would obstruct publication if sold to others, especially the British.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference Note on Sale of the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram reporting the sale of the Japan Advertiser to the Japan Times for $100,000.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: the Japan Advertiser was sold to the Japan Times at an agreed $100,000; see the September 12 telegram, file 894.918/34.

subfiles.title: Adviser’s Memorandum on the Japan Advertiser Sale
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Highlights evidence that the Japan Advertiser sale occurred under threats and an ultimatum backed by Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck advises remembering that the Japanese named the price, threats and an ultimatum backed the sale, and Go said a Foreign Office faction favored confiscation without compensation.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 965: Sale of the Japan Advertiser, Sections One and Two
subfiles.about: Reports the coerced $100,000 sale of the Japan Advertiser to the Japan Times and the negotiations immediately preceding it.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 965: Fleisher signed to transfer the Advertiser to Toshi Go for $100,000 payable in New York, assuming about $12,000 in staff bonuses; Grew calls it virtual confiscation under threats, recalls a larger German offer, notes Fleisher refused his intervention, and credits Matsuoka with full immediate payment.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1090: Withholding Press Releases from the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: Notifies the Department that press releases addressed to the now-sold Japan Advertiser are being withheld.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1090: Grew, citing the October telegram on the newspaper's sale, is withholding Department press releases for the Japan Advertiser pending instructions.

subfiles.title: Department Reply Approving Discontinuation of Japan Advertiser Press Releases
subfiles.about: Approves Grew’s decision and ends the forwarding of Department press releases intended for the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: State approves withholding press releases and says further sets for the Japan Advertiser won't be sent through the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Press Releases
subfiles.about: Recommends ending the exceptional provision of Department press releases to the Japan Advertiser after its sale.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs memo: supplying the Advertiser with press releases was an exceptional courtesy not extended to other American-owned or foreign papers; it endorses Grew's decision, and Mr. Fisher will stop the sets marked for the paper.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1352: Sale of the Japan Chronicle
subfiles.about: Reports British Embassy information concerning the sale of the Japan Chronicle to the publishers of the Japan Times and Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1352: the Japan Chronicle sold for about 150,000 yen with no objectionable pressure and intended continued publication; apart from the American-owned Japan News-Week, Japan's last foreign-owned newspaper disappears.

subfiles.title: Kobe Telegram Confirming the Japan Chronicle Sale
subfiles.about: Confirms that the Japan Chronicle’s sale to the Japan Times and Advertiser would soon be announced.
subfiles.summary: Kobe telegram confirms the sale of the Japan Chronicle, a long-established Kobe morning paper, probably to continue as an evening paper in Kobe.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 5408: Japan News-Week
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Assesses the ownership, finances, readership, editorial policy, and diplomatic value of the independently owned Japan News-Week.
subfiles.summary: Grew describes W. R. Wills’s weekly as Japan’s only remaining English-language publication owned and edited by a foreigner and rejects rumors that it received a Japanese subsidy. Supported largely by Japanese advertising, it remained only marginally profitable and faced shortages, police warnings, censorship, and pressure attributed partly to the German Embassy. Grew praises editor C. N. Spinks and the paper’s forceful pro-American, anti-Axis commentary, while noting its opposition to embargoes and criticism of United States policy toward the Soviet Union. He recommends support for the paper and encloses summaries, clippings, and a letter to Wills.

subfiles.title: Summary of Certain Editorial Articles Appearing in Recent Issues of the Japan News-Week
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japan News-Week editorials published between December 21, 1940, and February 22, 1941.
subfiles.summary: The summaries cover criticism of the Tripartite Alliance, Japan’s deteriorating relations with the United States and Britain, and the unresolved war in China. They also describe proposals for unofficial Japanese-American talks and the paper’s criticism of Cordell Hull for condemning Axis aggression while omitting Soviet aggression. Later editorials demand clearer statements of Japan’s aims and warn that Hitler sought to use the alliance to provoke a Japanese-American war.

subfiles.title: Inconsistency
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan cannot exclude foreign involvement in East Asia while using the Tripartite Alliance to restrict American action in Europe.
subfiles.summary: The editorial condemns Matsuoka’s attempt to make the Axis alliance the basis of relations with the United States. It maintains that American aid to Britain is America’s own concern and warns that subordinating Japanese-American relations to Germany and Italy will undermine Nomura’s mission.

subfiles.title: Looking Forward
subfiles.about: Reviews Japan’s grave diplomatic, military, fiscal, and economic prospects for 1941.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "Looking Forward": sober New Year statements by Konoe, Matsuoka, Kawada and Kobayashi on pressure, the China war's cost and controls; it rejects the Axis-as-oppressed-majority claim, names China as Japan's fundamental problem and urges avoiding new adventures.

subfiles.title: A Way Out?
subfiles.about: Proposes unofficial Japanese-American discussions as a possible means of escaping the diplomatic deadlock and preventing war.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "A Way Out?": Japan and America hold irreconcilable "immutable policies" toward a showdown; it revives unofficial business and civic leaders seeking common ground and Cornelius Whitney's Manila Pacific conference idea, possibly too late but among the last hopes.

subfiles.title: Fish & Fowl
subfiles.about: Criticizes Cordell Hull for condemning German, Italian, and Japanese aggression while omitting Soviet aggression.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "Fish & Fowl": accepts Hull's indictment of Axis expansion and Japan can't expect different treatment, but argues Soviet occupations in Poland, Finland, the Baltics and Romania are aggression too, so courting Moscow weakens America's case and feeds Japanese suspicions of bias.

subfiles.title: Understanding Japan
subfiles.about: Calls for clear explanations of Japanese policy and examines why Americans interpret Japan’s New Order as expansionist and totalitarian.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "Understanding Japan" welcomes Atsushi Akaike's Diet criticism of the Konoe Cabinet as proof debate survived, says vague descriptions of the New Structure and Co-Prosperity Sphere make Americans assume the worst, and urges Japan to state its purposes clearly.

subfiles.title: Words of Wrath
subfiles.about: Interprets Hitler’s threats against American shipping as an attempt to activate the Tripartite Alliance and draw Japan into war with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "Words of Wrath": Lease-Lend shows America's resolve to back Britain and Axis intimidation failing; Germany's position worsens after failing to beat Britain and Italy's African reverses; Hitler's shipping threats may prepare claims of American aggression to compel Japan under the Tripartite Alliance.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Obligation
subfiles.about: Welcomes the American reception of Ambassador Nomura while demanding a precise statement of Japan’s proposed New Order and its consequences.
subfiles.summary: Editorial "Japan's Obligation": Nomura's cordial Honolulu and San Francisco reception shows America still hoped for peace but suspected Japan demanded full acceptance of its New Order; Japan must explain its program concretely enough for America to judge.
